title: A cross-vertebrate single-cell and spatial atlas reveals evolutionary trajectories of gastrointestinal cellular innovation.
data_url: https://db.genomics.cn/stomics/gitomicsdb/download (GITomicsDB, a companion website in the STOmicsDB family). Files sit on an open web directory: https://ftp.cngb.org/pub/SciRAID/stomics/STDS0000400/ - 24 .h5ad files (AnnData/HDF5 single-cell matrices), 4.66 GB in total. Raw sequencing is separately in CNGBdb project CNP0007851 (not retrieved, never needed). Analysis code: github.com/BGI-Qingdao/GITomicsDB_project (GPL-3.0, Jupyter notebooks). Imaging validation on Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/20310497 (CC BY 4.0, 6 zip archives, 1,112,904,421 bytes of fluorescence and electron-microscopy images).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: The article itself is NOT in Europe PMC full text (1 hit, PMID 42612643, no PMCID, isOpenAccess=N, hasSuppl=N), and Crossref records the licence as CC BY-NC 4.0, published August 2026. NCBI elink from PubMed returned no GEO, SRA or BioProject links, and GEO searches for the species found nothing from this group, so I traced the data through the STOmicsDB collections page, which gave me GITomicsDB and the open file directory. (1) Directory listing read directly: 24 .h5ad files, sizes 29.69 MB to 2.11 GB, all dated 2026-05-25, total 4.66 GB; the server honours HTTP range requests. The 'lognorm' (log-normalised) files advertised on the site's Spatial and scRNA-seq browse pages return HTTP 404 and are not downloadable - only the raw-count files are. (2) I fully downloaded two files under my 50 MB limit and opened both with h5py: Lre.GI.scRNA.count.h5ad (39,539,944 bytes; lamprey gastrointestinal tract; dense matrix 11,907 cells x 18,913 genes, float32) and Cpl.Stomach.count.h5ad (31,132,406 bytes; bamboo-shark stomach Stereo-seq spatial data; sparse matrix 21,794 spots x 21,596 genes, 7,316,104 non-zero values, every sampled value a whole number between 1 and 96, with x/y/z coordinates and two annotation columns ann1 (7 classes, largest 'Oxynticopeptic' 7,365) and ann2 (9 classes)). (3) The 2.11 GB integrated atlas GIT.scRNA.count.h5ad (2,266,724,440 bytes) I did NOT download; I wrote a small HTTP-range reader and opened it remotely with h5py, pulling about 150 MB in 1 MiB slices across six probe runs. Verified in that file: matrix 935,520 cells x 7,038 genes, compressed-sparse-row, 448,713,771 non-zero values, raw whole-number counts (sampled range 1-876); the 7,038 gene names are upper-case HUMAN gene symbols (A3GALT2, AACS, AADAC ... ), i.e. the cross-species orthologue mapping is already done; 40 obs (per-cell) columns; the cell index is barcode+library, and all 935,520 values are unique (I read the whole index and counted). (4) Label columns I counted myself: 'cell type' 41 classes, 20 cells missing; 'cell compartment' 3 classes (Immune 381,157 / Epithelial 375,176 / Stromal 179,167); 'major cell type' 4 classes; level1_annot 8 classes; level2_annot 32 classes and level3_annot 84 classes, both missing for exactly 659,732 cells - which is every non-human cell, so the fine-grained labels are human-only. (5) Species counts (10 species): Homo sapiens 275,788; Pantodon buchholzi (African butterflyfish) 123,477; Polyodon spathula (American paddlefish) 108,360; Polypterus senegalus (gray bichir) 100,895; Oryzias melastigma (marine medaka) 100,251; Megalops atlanticus (Atlantic tarpon) 65,102; Atractosteus spatula (alligator gar) 61,354; Chiloscyllium plagiosum (white-spotted bamboo shark) 53,714; Protopterus annectens (African lungfish) 36,382; Lethenteron reissneri (lamprey) 10,197. 206 sequencing libraries, 6 to 18 per non-human species and 99 for human. (6) I ran the decisive check: I wrote a 41-to-18 class harmonisation dictionary and cross-tabulated it against species. Result: 12 classes have at least 200 cells in 7 or more of the 10 species (T/NK 10 species, Enterocyte 10, Myeloid 10, Endothelial 10, Stromal 9, B 9, Mucus 9, Goblet 9, Enteroendocrine 9, Tuft 9, Other-epithelial 7, BEST4 7). Ciliated cells have 200+ cells in only 4 species and are completely absent in human, medaka, butterflyfish and tarpon - the paper's 'ciliated cell loss' result is directly readable in the label column. (7) Counts reconcile exactly between files: the lamprey per-species file has 11,907 cells, and removing its Erythrocytes (1,277), Acinar (279) and Discard (154) rows gives 10,197, exactly the lamprey count in the integrated atlas. (8) obsm holds the authors' own precomputed integrations ready to use as features: Unintegrated (935,520 x 30), harmony (x30), scVI (x10), scanorama (x100), bbknn and two UMAP layouts. (9) The 'organ' column has case-duplicate categories: intestine 486,635 vs Small_intestine 11, and stomach 367,315 vs Stomach 9. (10) I resolved three of the human library identifiers through NCBI: GSM4546348 and GSM4546310 belong to GSE150290 (gastric cancer single-cell study, 52 samples) and GSM4766844 to GSE157477 (intestinal T lymphocytes from Crohn's disease and control patients). So the human arm is re-used published data from other labs, including diseased tissue, while all nine non-human species come from this one lab. (11) GitHub application programming interface on BGI-Qingdao/GITomicsDB_project: GPL-3.0, Jupyter Notebook, 2 stars, last pushed 2026-07-19, seven numbered analysis directories. (12) Zenodo application programming interface on record 20310497: CC BY 4.0, 6 zip files totalling 1,112,904,421 bytes of immunofluorescence and transmission-electron-microscopy images for lungfish gut and bichir stomach.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: I could not read the article at all beyond its abstract - it has no PubMed Central identifier and no Europe PMC full text, and I did not fetch the publisher page. So everything about methods, limitations, statistics and the authors' own stated open questions is unknown to me. Taken from the abstract and the GITomicsDB site description, not verified: the '935,984 cells' headline (the file I opened holds 935,520, a 464-cell gap I cannot explain); 'nearly 1 million cells', 'ten species', '500 million years' and 'four organ systems'; the claims about conserved gene co-expression modules, de novo gene emergence, lymphoid aggregates in lungfish and functional polarization of fish oxynticopeptic cells. I did not open the four largest per-species files, did not download the Zenodo images, did not retrieve the CNGBdb raw-data project CNP0007851 or check its access terms, and did not read the full text of any prior-work paper in the C2 audit - for those I read search-result titles and summaries only. I did not run any model, and no timing number below was measured.

a1_downloadable.note: Passes, verified by actually downloading. The files sit on an open web directory with no login, no access application and no registration; I pulled two of them in full and range-read a third. Two frictions, not failures: the companion site advertises log-normalised files that return HTTP 404, and no explicit file-level licence is posted (the article is CC BY-NC 4.0, the imaging deposit CC BY 4.0, the code GPL-3.0).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Passes. I read the label columns out of the file: 'cell type' (41 classes), 'cell compartment' (3), 'major cell type' (4) and level1/2/3_annot are all already per-cell columns, with only 20 of 935,520 cells unlabelled. One real but bounded cost: the vocabulary is not harmonised across species (human cells carry finer names such as 'T and NK cells' where fish carry 'T-like'), so you need a hand-written 41-to-about-14 class dictionary. That is a dictionary, not a construction of the target - I wrote one in ten minutes and it left 12 classes with 200+ cells in 7 or more species.

a3_inputs_present.note: Passes, and unusually cleanly. The input is the expression matrix itself, present in the file, and the 7,038 gene columns are already upper-case human gene symbols - the hard cross-species orthologue mapping that normally sinks this kind of project has been done by the authors. No identifier lookup is needed, and the symbols are exactly the input vocabulary that human-trained single-cell models expect.

a4_units_stated.note: Passes for the main task. The matrix holds raw unique-molecule counts (I confirmed every sampled value is a whole number, 1 to 876), and per-cell totals are given as n_counts / nCount_RNA with gene counts as nFeature_RNA. One gap: the spatial files' x/y/z columns have no stated unit (they look like Stereo-seq bin indices rather than micrometres), which matters only if you use the spatial data.

a5_enough_rows.note: Passes, and the count is mine, read from the matrix shape. The modelling unit is the cell (935,520 of them), but the unit that governs the headline question is the species, of which there are 10, plus 206 sequencing libraries for within-species grouping. The smallest species, lamprey, still has 10,197 cells, and 12 harmonised cell classes have 200+ cells in 7 or more species.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 2.27 GB for the one integrated file (2,266,724,440 bytes); about 3.6 GB in memory if you load the whole sparse matrix at once; under 1 GB after subsampling a few thousand cells per species and class; 4.66 GB if you ever want all 24 files
a6_fits_laptop.note: Passes, with the obvious subsetting route. One 2.27 GB download is the whole working set, which is small for an atlas because the authors already reduced it to 7,038 orthologous genes. Loading the full sparse matrix costs about 3.6 GB of memory; reading it in row chunks and keeping a stratified subsample keeps the peak near 2 GB on a 16 GB machine. The proposed baseline needs no graphics card. Note this breaks the scout tool's own 50 MB download rule, which is why I range-read rather than downloaded it.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Passes, with one small unexplained gap I am flagging rather than hiding. The file holds 935,520 cells; the abstract and the companion website both say 935,984, a difference of 464 cells (0.05%) that I cannot resolve without the full text. Everything internal reconciles exactly: the lamprey per-species file's 11,907 cells minus its Erythrocytes (1,277), Acinar (279) and Discard (154) rows gives precisely the 10,197 lamprey cells in the integrated atlas, which also tells you erythrocytes and pancreatic acinar cells were deliberately dropped from the integrated version.

a8_label_provenance.note: Passes, but this is the project's main intellectual risk and it must be stated plainly. The labels are expert manual annotation: the authors clustered each species' cells and then named the clusters from canonical marker genes. That is human judgement anchored on literature, not another model's prediction, so there is no distillation problem - but the clusters were computed from the same expression values that would be the model's input. The consequence is strict: a random within-species split would partly be predicting the authors' own clustering, so the only honest evaluation is leaving out a whole species (whose labels came from a separate clustering run and separate human judgement) or a whole library. Two semi-independent anchors exist: the Stereo-seq spatial annotations are a different assay on different tissue sections, and the fluorescence and electron-microscopy images on Zenodo were the authors' own wet-lab check.

B1.why: One file holds matrix and all 40 label columns row-aligned; verified by opening it.

B2.why: Opened on first try with h5py, locally and over HTTP range reads; no fixes needed.

B3.why: 41 class names not harmonised across species; human finer-grained; needs a hand dictionary.

B4.why: Only 20 of 935,520 cells lack a coarse label; counted. Fine labels are human-only by design.

B5.why: I read the whole cell index: 935,520 rows, 935,520 unique. No duplicates.

B6.why: No data dictionary; columns 'so', 'group1', 'celltypeBC' are guesses. Code repo would explain.

C1.why: Accuracy-versus-divergence-time decay is informative either way; no need to beat anyone.

C2.why: SATURN, SAMap, UCE, TranscriptFormer, scGPT open and benchmarked, but never on these nine species.

C3.why: Diversity plus unique application: 9 non-mammalian vertebrates, one organ, one label vocabulary.

C4.why: Manual marker-based annotation of 936,000 cells across 10 species is the expensive step replaced.

C5.why: TranscriptFormer publishes macro-F1 versus evolutionary distance; plus majority-class and marker-score dummies.

D1.why: scGPT and Geneformer weights are open and take human gene symbols, which the file's 7,038 columns already are.

D2.why: Frozen embeddings cacheable once, but a CPU pass over 100,000 cells is hours; GPU would help.

D3.why: Backbone licences permissive (MIT, Apache-2.0); article is CC BY-NC 4.0 and h5ad files carry no posted licence.

E1.why: Leave-one-species-out, or leave-one-library-out; both columns verified present in the file.

E2.why: 10 species and 206 libraries, counted; smallest species still 10,197 cells.

E3.why: Majority class after harmonisation is T/NK at 20.8%; per-species majority also available.

E4.why: No replicate cells, but three label columns disagree per cell and Stereo-seq re-annotates same tissues.

E5.why: Organ as trivial target; ATP4A/PGC in oxynticopeptic cells; verified ciliated absence in 4 species.

E6.why: Shuffle labels within library, random-noise features, gene-block ablation, shuffle-within-species.

E7.why: Six Stereo-seq sections are a held-out assay; human arm is other labs' GEO data; GSE240094 exists.

E8.why: No published number on this dataset; reproducing TranscriptFormer or UCE needs GPU-scale inference.

G1.why: Gene columns are human HGNC symbols, verified; plus NCBI taxonomy-resolvable species and GEO library IDs.

G2.why: CZ CELLxGENE Census and the human Gut Cell Atlas both join on human gene symbol, already present.

G3.why: Gene-symbol join near one-to-one but synonym-prone; mapping 41 classes to Cell Ontology is the messy part.

G4.why: Asks whether human-trained annotation transfers across 500 million years; neither dataset answers alone.

H1.why: All cells labelled, but absence of a class can mean biological loss or failed sampling; indistinguishable.

H2.why: 10 species, 206 libraries, but all 9 non-human from one lab; human re-used from other labs' studies.

H3.why: Honest claim writes out in one sentence, naming the one lab, the one organ and the human disease confound.

H4.why: Species and organ coverage spelled out on the site; the human-arm disease sources are not flagged anywhere.

I1.why: Named: the CZI TranscriptFormer team, the SATURN group, and any lab annotating a non-model organism.

I2.why: A failure stops people trusting zero-shot annotation on non-model species; a success saves weeks of curation.

I3.why: Decision is 'trust this automatic label for a new species?', so per-class macro F1 is the decision.

I4.why: A canonical-marker score may handle coarse classes; that dumb baseline must run first and may suffice.

J1.why: Grouped leave-one-species-out splits, class imbalance, frozen-backbone transfer: all the ML I want.

J2.why: Gut cell types are intuitive, but Mucus/Mucous/Foveolar and oxynticopeptic distinctions need reading.

J3.why: The harmonised cross-species label table and the decay curve are shareable even if models are mediocre.

J4.why: Three weeks is realistic given the data is already model-ready, but no budget is committed anywhere.

J5.why: Kill condition is nameable (marker-score lookup not beaten) but is not yet written into NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: TranscriptFormer (bioRxiv 2025, Chan Zuckerberg Initiative) - a generative single-cell model trained across species spanning 1.5 billion years of evolution
existing_models.score_and_split: From search-result summaries only, not retrieved in full: reports cell-type classification macro F1 (a per-class average accuracy measure) as a function of evolutionary distance from human, using leave-one-species-out evaluation, and claims robust performance for species separated by over 685 million years. This is the closest published analogue to the project I am proposing. I did not run it and verified no number.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved verbatim. The summaries present larger evolutionary distances as the hard regime, which is exactly where this dataset sits, and none of its training species is one of the nine non-mammalian vertebrates here.

existing_models.name: UCE (Universal Cell Embedding, Nature 2026) - a foundation model trained on about 36 million cells across 8 species that embeds new cells with no training or labelling
existing_models.score_and_split: From search-result summaries only: produces coherent zero-shot embeddings even for very divergent species such as Drosophila, and supports cell-type label transfer to species absent from training. Numbers and splits not retrieved, nothing run.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Reported in the summaries as the authors' own limitation: fine-grained label transfer across large evolutionary distances remains challenging. That is precisely the gap this dataset probes.

existing_models.name: SATURN (Nature Methods 2024) - cross-species single-cell integration that encodes each gene by a protein-language-model embedding so datasets can be joined without one-to-one orthologues
existing_models.score_and_split: From summaries only: beats SAMap, the previous best, at producing clusters that match conserved cell types, and transfers annotations between evolutionarily remote species. No number verified, nothing run.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved. Relevant structural limitation for this dataset: SATURN needs protein sequences per species, which this deposit does not include - a genuine extra cost if you want to use it.

existing_models.name: SAMap - cross-species single-cell mapping using protein-sequence similarity together with expression correlation
existing_models.score_and_split: From summaries only: described as the strongest baseline for atlas-level integration beyond the family level. No number verified, nothing run.

existing_models.name: Benchmarking cross-species single-cell integration (Nucleic Acids Research 2025) - a published comparison of 9 integration methods over 20 species, 4.7 million cells and 8 phyla
existing_models.score_and_split: From summaries only: all methods decline in both biological-signal preservation and batch correction as phylogenetic distance grows, partly because fewer one-to-one orthologues survive; SATURN is the most robust across taxonomic levels, SAMap best beyond family level. This is honest evaluation already done, which is why I scored C2 as 1 and not 2.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved verbatim; the stated cause - shrinking orthologue sets at distance - is itself a named open problem, and notably this dataset side-steps it by shipping a fixed 7,038-gene human-symbol space.

existing_models.name: scGPT and Geneformer - the two best-known single-cell foundation models, evaluated without fine-tuning in Genome Biology 2025 ('Zero-shot evaluation reveals limitations of single-cell foundation models')
existing_models.score_and_split: From summaries only: in zero-shot use neither consistently beats simpler methods - scVI, Harmony, or even just highly variable genes - at separating cell types or removing batch effects. A published, honest negative result, and a ready-made baseline framing.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The paper's own point: zero-shot utility is unproven and batch effects are unhandled. Species identity here is the largest batch effect imaginable, which makes this dataset a natural extension of their test.

existing_models.name: CellTypist - lightweight logistic-regression cell-type classifiers, including models trained on the human gut, that take human gene symbols as input
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved in this round; I name it because it is the one existing model I could genuinely run in an afternoon on a 16 GB CPU laptop, and the file's gene columns are already the human symbols it expects. Its published human-gut accuracy would be the number to transfer from.

existing_models.name: Any model trained or tested on this specific atlas
existing_models.score_and_split: I found none in four searches, which is unsurprising for an August 2026 paper, so call it likely absent rather than absent. The authors' own code repository (GPL-3.0, 7 notebook directories) does clustering, three integration strategies, gene-module and trajectory analysis - no supervised classifier.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Unknown: I could not read the article's discussion, because it has no open full text.

backbone.name: scGPT or Geneformer, both single-cell transcriptome models with open weights that take human gene symbols as their input vocabulary - which is exactly what the file's 7,038 gene columns already are, so no mapping work is needed. CellTypist (a set of small open logistic-regression classifiers, including human gut models) is the cheap first comparison, and the authors' own precomputed scVI (10-dimensional) and Harmony (30-dimensional) coordinates in the file give a free third feature set.
backbone.hardware: 16 GB CPU laptop is enough. Stratified subsample of about 100,000 cells (10,000 per species), cache frozen embeddings once - my estimate is roughly 3 hours at 10 cells per second, not timed - then train a linear or gradient-boosted head in minutes. The no-backbone baseline (log-normalised counts plus logistic regression) needs no embedding step at all. Only a comparison against TranscriptFormer or UCE would really want a graphics card.
backbone.licence: Backbone side is clean: scGPT code is MIT, Geneformer is on HuggingFace under Apache-2.0, CellTypist is open. Data side is the flag: the article's Crossref licence is CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial), the h5ad files carry no posted file-level licence, the imaging deposit is CC BY 4.0 and the analysis code is GPL-3.0. Fine for a personal or academic project; ask before any commercial use.

integration.partner_dataset: CZ CELLxGENE Census - an open, programmatically queryable corpus of roughly 100 million annotated human and mouse cells, including large healthy gut collections - and, more narrowly, the human Gut Cell Atlas (Elmentaite et al.), which is the training source behind CellTypist's gut models.
integration.join_key: Human gene symbol. The atlas's 7,038 gene columns are already upper-case human symbols (I read them), so the feature spaces intersect directly with no new identifier mapping. Secondary keys: NCBI taxonomy identifiers for the 10 species, and GEO sample identifiers for the 99 human libraries. The one-to-many care point is the label vocabulary, not the genes: 41 class names must be collapsed onto Cell Ontology terms before any comparison, and symbol synonyms will silently drop a few hundred genes.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a cell-type classifier trained on the tens of millions of human and mouse cells in a public census still recognise the homologous cell types in a lamprey, shark or lungfish gut, and does its accuracy fall off predictably with divergence time - so that we could say in advance how far a human-trained annotator can be trusted on a non-model organism?

controls.positive_control: Three, chosen before looking at results. (1) Swap the label for organ (stomach versus intestine), which must come out near-perfect from expression - if it does not, the plumbing is wrong. (2) The model must score oxynticopeptic (acid- and pepsin-secreting) cells high on ATP4A and PGC, the two genes the authors themselves used as fluorescence probes. (3) Ciliated cells are present in paddlefish (15,206 cells) and bichir (10,300) and completely absent in human, medaka, butterflyfish and tarpon - a model trained without paddlefish must still find them in bichir, and must not invent them in human.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the cell-type labels within each library and confirm collapse to the majority class (T/NK cells, 20.8% of cells after harmonisation); replace the expression features with random noise of the same shape; ablate feature blocks (immune genes only, epithelial genes only); and shuffle within species rather than globally to confirm the leave-one-species-out grouping is actually grouping. The last one matters most here, because a random cell-level split would partly be predicting the authors' own clustering.
controls.external_validation: Unusually well supplied. (1) The six Stereo-seq spatial files are a different assay on different tissue sections of three of the same species, with their own independent annotations (ann1/ann2) - a true held-out platform. (2) The 99 human libraries come from other labs' published studies, so human is already an external cohort. (3) CZ CELLxGENE Census and the human Gut Cell Atlas are independent human references. (4) An existing lungfish respiratory atlas (GEO GSE240094, 48 samples, same species, different organ, different lab) tests whether the model's lungfish cell types hold up outside the gut.

honest_claim_h3: Given raw counts over 7,038 human-symbol orthologous genes, a classifier trained on nine vertebrate gut atlases can recover the authors' own marker-based coarse cell-type calls in a tenth, held-out species at X macro F1 - a claim about reproducing one lab's annotation of one organ in captive or farmed specimens, where the human comparison point is re-used data from gastric-cancer and Crohn's-disease studies on a different sequencing chemistry, and where a cell type's absence cannot be distinguished from a failure to sample it.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a gut cell's gene activity to predict its cell type in a species the model has never seen.
plain_idea.train_on: For each cell, the number of messenger-RNA molecules counted for each of 7,038 genes that have been matched one-to-one across all ten animals (so the gene columns mean the same thing in a lamprey and in a human). I verified 935,520 cells from 10 species and 206 sequencing runs.
plain_idea.predict: Which of about 14 gut cell types the cell is - absorptive enterocyte, mucus-producing goblet cell, T cell, acid-secreting stomach cell, and so on. The true answer is the authors' own expert label: they grouped similar cells together and named each group from well-known marker genes, which is interpretation of the same measurement rather than an independent assay - the reason the test must always be a whole species the model never trained on.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Anyone studying a non-model animal currently annotates cells by hand because nobody knows whether automatic annotators trained on human and mouse still work hundreds of millions of years away; this dataset gives a clean ladder from jawless fish to human in a single organ, so the answer is useful whichever way it comes out - either it saves weeks of curation per project, or it tells the field exactly how far these tools can be trusted.

ml_idea: Leave-one-species-out cell-type classification across 500 million years of vertebrate evolution, framed as a decay curve rather than a leaderboard. Train on nine species' gut cells (7,038 human-symbol orthologous genes, raw counts, already in one file) and predict the harmonised coarse cell type in the tenth, then plot macro F1 against divergence time from the training set. Four feature sets, cheapest first: (a) log-normalised counts plus logistic regression; (b) CellTypist's human gut models applied zero-shot, which is possible with no work at all because the gene columns are already human symbols; (c) the authors' own precomputed scVI and Harmony coordinates, already in the file; (d) frozen scGPT or Geneformer embeddings with a linear head. The result is informative either way: if a human-trained annotator labels lamprey myeloid cells correctly, that is a strong statement about deep conservation of transcriptional identity; if it fails at a specific node, that node becomes the interesting biology. Three things I verified make this unusually tractable. First, the hard part of cross-species work - building the orthologue space - is already done and the gene names are human symbols, which is exactly the input vocabulary the open models expect. Second, after a 41-to-14 class harmonisation dictionary that took me ten minutes, 12 classes still have 200+ cells in 7 or more species, so the task is a real multi-class problem and not a two-class toy. Third, the label table already contains a built-in positive control: ciliated cells exist in paddlefish and bichir and are flatly absent in human, medaka, butterflyfish and tarpon, so the model has to reproduce a presence/absence pattern, not just a frequency. Two traps that must be handled up front. The human arm is not a healthy reference - I resolved three of its library identifiers to a gastric-cancer study (GSE150290) and a Crohn's-disease T-cell study (GSE157477) - and it is the only arm on a different sequencing chemistry from a different lab, so species effect and platform effect are confounded precisely at the human end; the clean version of the experiment either drops human from training or reports both. And the labels come from clustering the same matrix, so any within-species random split is partly circular and the whole design has to be grouped by species or library. A secondary project with the same files: use the six Stereo-seq spatial sections as a held-out assay, training on dissociated cells and predicting the spatial annotations - that tests transfer across platform rather than across species, and it is the cheapest honest external validation I have seen in this batch of candidates.

effort.compute_note: Sizes are measured, not estimated: the directory listing and HTTP headers gave exact byte counts (2,266,724,440 for the integrated file), and I read the matrix shape (935,520 x 7,038) and non-zero count (448,713,771) out of the file itself, which gives 3.6 GB in memory at 8 bytes per stored value - hence peak_ram_gb of 4 for a naive full load, or about 2 GB with chunked reading. hours_to_feature_table is the 2.3 GB download plus writing the 41-class harmonisation dictionary and fixing the duplicate 'intestine'/'Small_intestine' categories; the matrix itself needs no cleaning. embedding_hours assumes a 100,000-cell stratified subsample through scGPT or Geneformer on an Apple-silicon CPU at an assumed 10 cells per second; nothing was timed. cv_run_minutes is ten leave-one-species-out folds of logistic regression on that subsample. The first pass (logistic regression plus CellTypist) needs no embedding step at all.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count cells per species per harmonised cell class - and I already ran it, so this project's cheapest killer is answered: 12 classes keep 200+ cells in 7 or more of the 10 species, so the task survives. The remaining cheapest check, which I did not finish and which should be done first, is to resolve all 99 human library identifiers through NCBI and see how many belong to datasets that CellTypist's gut models or the Gut Cell Atlas were trained on. I resolved three and two were a gastric-cancer study, one a Crohn's-disease study; if most of the human arm is CellTypist training data, the human fold leaks and human must be dropped from the zero-shot comparison entirely.

verdict_reason: Everything that normally kills a cross-species single-cell project has already been done by the authors, and I verified it in the files rather than trusting the abstract - which I could not read anyway, since this paper has no open full text. One 2.27 GB file holds 935,520 cells from 10 species over a fixed 7,038-gene space whose column names are already upper-case human gene symbols; the labels are per-cell columns with only 20 cells unlabelled; the cell index is 935,520 rows and 935,520 unique; the counts are raw whole numbers; and the authors' own scVI, Harmony and Scanorama coordinates are sitting in the same file as free alternative features. I opened two files in full locally and read the big one over HTTP range requests without downloading it. The orthologue mapping - the step that the published Nucleic Acids Research benchmark blames for the decay of every existing method at distance - is pre-solved here, which is why the effort is a few days rather than a few months. The angle is diversity plus unique application and it is strong enough to override the project's own size filter: nine of the ten species (lamprey, bamboo shark, paddlefish, alligator gar, bichir, tarpon, butterflyfish, medaka, lungfish) appear in no foundation model's training corpus, they sit on a clean phylogenetic ladder in a single organ with one annotation vocabulary, and UCE's and TranscriptFormer's authors both name fine-grained transfer at large evolutionary distance as the unsolved part. C2 is a 1, not a 2, and honestly so: SATURN, SAMap, UCE, TranscriptFormer, scGPT and Geneformer all have open weights, TranscriptFormer already publishes a macro-F1-versus-evolutionary-distance curve using leave-one-species-out, and a 20-species benchmark exists - but none of them has seen these species, which makes this an external test set rather than a crowded leaderboard. C1 is a 2 because the decay curve cannot produce a useless answer. Two caveats to carry into the write-up, both discovered in the files. First, A8: the labels are the authors' marker-based naming of their own clusters, so a random within-species split would partly be predicting that clustering - the design must group by species or by library, and I pass A8 only on that condition. Second, the human arm is not a healthy reference and not comparable in chemistry: I resolved three of its 99 library identifiers and found a gastric-cancer study (GSE150290) and a Crohn's-disease T-cell study (GSE157477), while all nine non-human species come from this one lab, so species and platform are confounded exactly at the human end. Neither is fatal; both change what the model may claim. Minor flags: the website advertises log-normalised files that return HTTP 404, the headline cell count is 935,984 against the file's 935,520, there is no column dictionary, and the article is CC BY-NC 4.0 with no file-level licence posted. Do it, and start by resolving the remaining human library identifiers before trusting any human-to-fish zero-shot number.
